Trying to Conceive

Heavy periods: recognising the problem and choosing treatment

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Periods vary, but bleeding that disrupts your life or leaves you exhausted deserves attention. You do not need to measure an exact amount before asking for help, and treatment can address both the bleeding and its effects.

Heavy bleeding is about its effect on your life

Heavy menstrual bleeding, sometimes called menorrhagia, means periods that cause problems because of the amount or duration of bleeding. You do not need to prove an exact volume before asking for help. Missing work, avoiding activities, disturbed sleep or constantly planning around leaks are important symptoms in their own right.

Research has often used more than eighty millilitres of blood per cycle as a threshold. Eighty millilitres is not an upper limit on how much someone can lose. Commonly quoted average volumes, such as thirty to forty millilitres, are not a practical home target, because menstrual fluid and product absorbency vary.

Useful signs include soaking products every one to two hours, using extra protection, bleeding through clothing or bedding, passing clots larger than about 2.5 centimetres or bleeding for more than seven days. The number of pads alone is imperfect: changing for comfort is different from completely soaking one.

Know when you need help immediately

Bleeding that soaks a pad or tampon about every hour for several hours needs prompt medical advice. If heavy bleeding is accompanied by fainting, marked dizziness, chest pain, shortness of breath, collapse or feeling seriously unwell, seek emergency care. Do not wait to reach a precise product count or two-hour threshold if you already have severe symptoms.

Severe abdominal or pelvic pain also changes the urgency, especially if pregnancy is possible. Use the local emergency number or urgent-care service rather than waiting for a routine menstrual appointment. Have someone help you travel if you feel faint; do not drive yourself.

For a stable but persistently heavy pattern, arrange an appointment rather than accepting it indefinitely. Severe cramps, bleeding between periods or after sex, and pain with sex, urination or bowel movements deserve discussion. You can ask for treatment while the cause and any effects of blood loss are assessed.

Bleeding related to pregnancy is not an ordinary period

A miscarriage can sometimes look like an unusually heavy or late period. An ectopic pregnancy, in which a pregnancy develops outside the uterus, can cause bleeding and pain and may become life-threatening. The amount of vaginal bleeding does not reliably show how much bleeding is happening internally.

If pregnancy is possible, tell the clinician and consider a pregnancy test, but do not delay urgent care to obtain one. One-sided lower abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, severe dizziness or fainting needs urgent assessment even without a previous positive result. Symptoms, examination, ultrasound and blood tests may all contribute to the diagnosis.

Bleeding after giving birth is also different from menstruation. Heavy or increasing postpartum bleeding, large clots, fever, faintness or feeling unwell needs prompt maternity advice. Later returning periods may differ from before pregnancy, but “you recently had a baby” is not enough to dismiss severe bleeding.

Hormonal changes can alter the pattern

Ovulation and the changing effects of oestrogen and progesterone influence how the uterine lining builds and sheds. When ovulation is irregular, the lining may shed unpredictably and sometimes heavily. This is more complex than diagnosing “too much oestrogen” from the appearance of a period.

Cycles can change when periods first begin, around the transition to menopause, after pregnancy or after starting or stopping hormonal contraception. Conditions affecting ovulation, including polycystic ovary syndrome, can also contribute. An underactive thyroid is another possible cause when the overall symptoms suggest thyroid disease.

A heavier first day or one unusually heavy month does not identify a particular cause. Likewise, repeated heavy cycles do not prove a single hormonal problem. Describe the pattern and relevant changes in medicines, contraception or health rather than assigning causes according to which day is heaviest.

Structural conditions and pelvic pain need consideration

Polyps are growths from the uterine lining that can contribute to bleeding. Fibroids are non-cancerous growths of uterine muscle. Their size and location matter: a fibroid affecting the cavity may cause different problems from one growing mainly toward the outside of the uterus.

Adenomyosis involves endometrial-type tissue within the muscle of the uterine wall and can be associated with heavy, painful periods. Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the uterine lining outside the uterus and commonly causes period-related pelvic pain; some people also report heavy bleeding or lower-back pain.

These conditions can coexist, and symptoms alone may not distinguish them. A painful period does not automatically mean endometriosis, and finding a small fibroid does not establish that it explains everything. The clinician considers the examination, symptoms and appropriate investigations together before choosing treatment.

Medicines, contraception and bleeding disorders matter

A copper IUD can make periods heavier, particularly after insertion. A hormonal intrauterine system is different and may be used to reduce heavy bleeding. If bleeding is new or troublesome with either device, ask for assessment rather than removing it yourself or assuming every IUD has the same effect.

Anticoagulants and some other medicines can increase bleeding. Bring a full medicine list, including aspirin, supplements and recent changes. Do not stop a prescribed anticoagulant independently; the prescriber can help balance bleeding control against the reason the medicine is needed.

A bleeding disorder such as von Willebrand disease may make it harder for bleeding to stop. Mention heavy periods since they first began, easy bruising, frequent nosebleeds, prolonged bleeding after dental work or surgery and relevant family history. Testing is guided by that history; a single prevalence figure does not predict whether you have a disorder.

Cancer is an uncommon cause, but certain changes must be checked

Most heavy periods are not caused by cancer. Nevertheless, abnormal bleeding can be associated with disease of the uterine lining or cervix, including cancer. It is not useful to present uterine, cervical and ovarian cancers as equally likely explanations for a heavy period.

Bleeding between periods, after sex or after menopause should be reported. Once menopause has occurred, even a small amount of bleeding on one occasion needs assessment. Do not label it a returning period without medical advice.

Age, the bleeding pattern, medicines and other risk factors help determine which investigations are appropriate. The aim is neither automatic cancer testing for every person nor reassurance based only on a common life stage. Ask what possible causes the assessment is intended to rule out and when results should arrive.

Prepare for a focused assessment

A useful record includes cycle dates, duration, fully soaked products, leaks, clot size, pain and the effect on daily activities. Tell the clinician whether pregnancy is possible, whether you want future pregnancy and what treatment outcomes matter most to you. You do not have to wait several cycles to begin this conversation.

A full blood count checks for anaemia and is routinely recommended for heavy menstrual bleeding. Other testing depends on the history. Clotting tests may be appropriate when a bleeding disorder is suspected; thyroid testing is generally reserved for additional suggestive symptoms, and a broad hormone panel is not routinely needed.

An examination, ultrasound, hysteroscopy to look inside the uterus or a sample of the lining may be recommended for particular findings or risks. Not everyone needs every test. Ask what each procedure can show, how discomfort will be managed and whether treatment can start while you wait for investigation.

Medicines can reduce bleeding and treat its effects

Options include a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system, combined hormonal contraception or selected progestogen treatments. These have different effects on bleeding, contraception and side effects. A treatment used for bleeding control may also prevent pregnancy while you use it, which should be part of the choice.

Non-hormonal options include tranexamic acid and suitable anti-inflammatory medicines, such as certain NSAIDs. NSAIDs can reduce menstrual bleeding and cramps for some people but are unsuitable in some circumstances, including particular bleeding, stomach or kidney problems. Do not combine painkillers or use someone else’s prescription.

Tranexamic acid also requires a suitability check, especially with a history of blood clots, kidney problems, irregular unexplained bleeding or pregnancy possibility. Iron treatment may be needed for iron deficiency or anaemia, but iron alone does not control the cause of bleeding. Ask when treatment should help and how response will be reviewed.

Procedures and follow-up should fit your priorities

Removing a polyp or treating a fibroid may reduce bleeding when it is responsible. Options depend on location, size and symptoms. More extensive treatments, including endometrial ablation or hysterectomy, have important consequences and should follow a discussion of alternatives, risks and future pregnancy plans.

Endometrial ablation is not suitable if you want a future pregnancy, and contraception is still needed afterward because pregnancy can occur and be dangerous. Hysterectomy removes the uterus and permanently ends the ability to carry a pregnancy. These are not interchangeable with procedures intended to preserve the uterus.

Review both the bleeding and how you feel: energy, pain, daily activity and any anaemia matter. If treatment is ineffective, poorly tolerated or no longer fits your plans, return to discuss another approach. Heavy periods are a valid reason to seek care, and a clear follow-up plan is part of treatment rather than an optional extra.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Quality-of-life effects matter alongside bleeding amount and duration.

Pregnancy-related and postmenopausal bleeding need their own assessment.

Testing and treatment should reflect the history, health risks and reproductive goals.

How BeMama can help

Bring a simple bleeding record and name your main priorities, such as less pain, fewer leaks, more predictable periods or preserving future pregnancy options.

When to seek help

Seek emergency care for heavy bleeding with faintness, chest pain, breathing difficulty, collapse or severe pain. Possible pregnancy with one-sided or shoulder-tip pain also needs urgent assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Eighty millilitres is not a maximum blood loss or a home test you must complete.
  • An hourly soaked product pattern needs prompt advice.
  • Copper and hormonal intrauterine devices have different effects.
  • Do not stop prescribed blood thinners without advice.
  • Treatment choices should include their effects on future pregnancy.

Frequently asked questions

Must I measure eighty millilitres before seeking help?

No. The effect on your life, bleeding pattern and symptoms are enough to start an assessment.

Does a heavy first day identify the cause?

No. Timing alone cannot distinguish hormones, structural conditions, medicines or other causes.

Could a heavy period actually be pregnancy bleeding?

Yes. Miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy can resemble a period. Possible pregnancy with pain or faintness needs urgent assessment.

Are heavy periods after birth always normal?

No. Postpartum bleeding and later returning periods need to be distinguished, and severe or worsening bleeding should not be dismissed.

Do all IUDs make periods heavier?

No. Copper IUDs can increase bleeding, while a hormonal intrauterine system may reduce it.

Should I stop my anticoagulant?

Do not stop it independently. Ask the prescriber for a plan that addresses bleeding and the condition being treated.

Does everyone need thyroid and hormone tests?

No. A full blood count is routine, while thyroid, clotting and other tests are selected for the clinical history.

Can NSAIDs reduce menstrual bleeding?

They can help some people, but suitability depends on medicines and health conditions. Ask before using them if you have bleeding, stomach or kidney problems.

Does endometrial ablation prevent pregnancy?

No. It is not contraception; pregnancy afterward can be dangerous, and it is unsuitable when future pregnancy is desired.

Is one small bleed after menopause worth checking?

Yes. Even a small amount or a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding needs medical assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
